ety.text: From Middle English gon, igon, gan, ȝegan, from Old English gān, ġegān, from Proto-Germanic *gānaz (“gone”), past participle of *gāną (“to go”). Cognate with West Germanic Scots gane (“gone”), West Frisian gien (“gone”), Low German gahn (“gone”), and Dutch gegaan (“gone”).

ex: The days of my youth are gone.
All hopes for a truce are gone.
I'm afraid all the coffee is gone.
If the milk is all gone, we'll drink our coffee black.
The bulb is gone. Can you put a new one in?
The car isn't driveable — the steering is gone.
Have you seen the company's revenue? It's through the floor. They're gone.

senses.d: Not fully aware of one's surroundings, often through intoxication or mental decline.
ex: Don't bother trying to understand what Grandma says; she's gone.
[S]he put on a kind of sing-song voice whenever she was pissed, it was one of the signs that she was really gone[…].

senses.d: Infatuated; in love (+ on, for, in).
ex: I am, of course, ‘gone’ for you.
But he was pleased and happy and flattered. She was evidently frightfully gone on him.
It was a group of real gone cats.
Dad, I want to be a jock. All a jock needs is some hep patter and a real gone image. Now, they just don't teach that jazz in college.
You'd better hurry up, it's gone four o'clock.

fr:parti.gl: divided into two equal parts vertically, per pale; said of an escutcheon

ety.text: From andarsi + -ne. Compare French s'en aller, Catalan anar-se'n and to a lesser extent Spanish irse and andarse.
